syllabus.clause: WAL + memtable, flush to immutable sorted runs (SSTables), newest-first reads with Bloom filters and fence pointers, tombstones

at.step: Every write is appended to a write-ahead log before anything else happens, so a crash between landing in memory and reaching its real home can still be recovered by replaying the log in order.
The write also lands in an in-memory sorted structure, the memtable, which serves new writes and reads directly — it's consulted on every read, so nothing logged is ever invisible to a query.

The full memtable is flushed out as one new, immutable sorted run. A fresh, empty memtable takes over immediately, and the write-ahead log behind the flushed memtable can be discarded, since its data now lives safely on disk.
A read checks the memtable first, then every on-disk run from newest to oldest, stopping at the first match it finds.

Checking every run for every read doesn't scale. A Bloom filter per run answers definitely-not-here or maybe-here from memory, skipping a run's disk read entirely on a definite no; a fence pointer narrows a maybe down to the one range worth reading.

A delete can't remove anything in place, because the run holding the old value is immutable. It's recorded instead as its own kind of entry, a tombstone, which has to outrank and hide that older value on every read until a compaction physically drops both of them together.

items.item: Topics 26-27 made in-place updates cheaper; this topic doesn't compete on that axis at all — it eliminates in-place updates entirely, which is a different trade, not a better version of the same one.

at.step: Every technique so far still updates a page in place, paying its I/O cost immediately on every write. The next structure refuses that trade entirely: never update in place, write sequentially, and pay the cost back later, on its own schedule.

items.item: A write-ahead log's entire reason to exist is the narrow window between a write landing in volatile memory and reaching durable storage anywhere else — it protects nothing once a flush has already happened.

at.step: Every write is appended to a write-ahead log before anything else happens, so a crash between landing in memory and reaching its real home can still be recovered by replaying the log in order.

items.item: The memtable is not an optimization layer a correct implementation could skip — a read that bypassed it would return provably stale data for anything written since the last flush, which is a correctness bug, not a performance one.

at.step: The write also lands in an in-memory sorted structure, the memtable, which serves new writes and reads directly — it's consulted on every read, so nothing logged is ever invisible to a query.

items.item: A flushed run's immutability is the single property every later mechanic in this topic depends on: a Bloom filter built once for it stays correct forever, and a fence pointer's stored range never needs updating, specifically because nothing in the run it describes can ever change.

at.step: The full memtable is flushed out as one new, immutable sorted run. A fresh, empty memtable takes over immediately, and the write-ahead log behind the flushed memtable can be discarded, since its data now lives safely on disk.

items.item: Newest-first reads aren't a performance tweak layered on top of a simpler correct algorithm — they are the only correct algorithm, since nothing else in the structure tracks which of several surviving copies of a key is current.

at.step: A read checks the memtable first, then every on-disk run from newest to oldest, stopping at the first match it finds.

items.item: A Bloom filter and a fence pointer are independent, compounding optimizations that answer two different questions (should this run be opened at all; where inside it to look), which is why a real system uses both rather than treating either as a substitute for the other.

items.item: A tombstone has to be at least as discoverable as the value it shadows, which is exactly why it's stored and indexed like any other write rather than as out-of-band metadata — anything less discoverable would let an older value resurface on some reads and not others.

at.step: A delete can't remove anything in place, because the run holding the old value is immutable. It's recorded instead as its own kind of entry, a tombstone, which has to outrank and hide that older value on every read until a compaction physically drops both of them together.

items.item: A Bloom filter's guarantee only runs in one direction: it can say maybe about a key that is actually absent (a false positive), but it structurally cannot say definitely-not about a key that is actually present — reversing that asymmetry would silently lose real data.

items.item: Sequence numbers, not wall-clock timestamps, are what make 'newest wins' well-defined even across a crash and restart — a clock can run backward or stall across a failure, but a strictly increasing counter attached to every write cannot.
